title: All five doodles (simulated)
blurb: A made-up field with a pretend Planet X, to show every doodle shape.
story: SIMULATED, not real data. Nobody has found a zigzag in SPHEREx pictures yet, so this made-up patch of sky shows what one would look like: a pretend planet 500 times farther from the Sun than Earth, jumping 14 arcminutes back and forth between four visits six months apart. The field also holds a pretend fast star, asteroid, comet and variable star. The doodles below were found by the same automatic search that runs on the real pictures.

doodles.explain: It appears to jump about 796 arcseconds back and forth between visits six months apart. SPHEREx looks at each patch of sky from opposite sides of Earth's orbit, so a body far beyond Neptune would do exactly that. If it is real, the size of the jump puts it roughly 518 times as far from the Sun as Earth is. (Simulated object: it was put into this made-up field on purpose.)

A fuzzy object with a glow around it that moved 90 arcseconds (14.7 SPHEREx pixels) toward the north-west in 98 minutes, about 55 arcseconds per hour, while the stars stayed put. Only bodies inside our Solar System cross the sky that fast: an asteroid, or a comet if it looks fuzzy. (Simulated object: it was put into this made-up field on purpose.)

A point of light that moved 66 arcseconds (10.7 SPHEREx pixels) toward the north-east in 98 minutes, about 40 arcseconds per hour, while the stars stayed put. Only bodies inside our Solar System cross the sky that fast: an asteroid, or a comet if it looks fuzzy. (Simulated object: it was put into this made-up field on purpose.)

This one is always there but slides steadily toward the north-east: 12.3 arcseconds (2.0 SPHEREx pixels) in 18 months, about 8.2 arcseconds a year. Steady drift like this is how a nearby star or brown dwarf looks from Earth. (Simulated object: it was put into this made-up field on purpose.)

It stays in the same place but brightened by about 91% between visits, after allowing for the different infrared colour of each exposure. Stars that pulse, flare or get eclipsed do this. (Simulated object: it was put into this made-up field on purpose.)
